new_statements.rule_in_words: Branch-level (Pearic) statement covering Somray of Battambang and Samre of Siem Reap among ten dialects: the word is one stressed main syllable, optionally preceded by a weakly stressed presyllable with a neutral vowel; i.e. stress is on the final (main) syllable of the sesquisyllabic word, predictable from syllable type. No Somray-specific prosodic statement exists in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; presyllable reduced to zero in some Thai Chong dialects (not Somray). Martin 1975 p. 90 notes Somray disyllables often lose their first element ([cənluh] > [nluh]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word (canonic word shape in a comparative phonology); based on wordlists/citation forms (Baradat 1941 ms., Martin 1974a,b, Huffman ms.). Genus-level generalization, not a description of Somray as such.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog somr1240 [smu] bundles Somray of Kranhung, Battambang (Martin's SY, Baradat's West Pear WP; Headley 1985 'North Central' group) with the extinct Somre of Siem Reap (Moura 1883 wordlist only). Martin's 1974b 'Esquisse phonologique du somree' actually describes the Somree of Peam Prus/Anlong Krauch, Pursat Province, which Headley 1985 classifies with 'Samre of Pursat' (his South Central 4.1), i.e. closer to the Samre [sxm] of Ploykaew 2001 (Glottolog samr1245, Trat refugees from the Pursat side) than to Battambang Somray; Glottolog nevertheless files Martin 1974 under somr1240, and Ethnologue places smu in both Pursat and Battambang. The deciding statement quoted here is Headley's Pearic-wide canonic word shape, with Somray of Battambang and Samre of Siem Reap explicitly among the ten dialects it covers; treat as genus-level (pear1246 / west2394), not a Somray-specific description.
